questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's pre-merge job runs `claude -p "Review this diff and return findings as JSON" --output-format json`, and a script pipes the reply through `jq` to count blocking findings. About 6% of runs fail because the reply wraps the findings in a sentence or a code fence. The pipeline needs machine-readable findings, and the check must not slow the merge. What should the team change?

options.text: Add two example replies in raw JSON, with no code fence, to the prompt, and keep the `jq` step as it is.
options.explanation: Examples make the format more likely but give no guarantee, so some share of runs would still wrap the reply. A pipeline that counts blocking findings needs the format enforced.

options.text: Add a regular expression before the `jq` step that strips leading text and code fences from the reply, so only the findings object remains.
options.explanation: The regular expression hides the symptom but not the cause. Any new wrapper, a missing field or a changed key still breaks the pipeline, because nothing defines the findings' structure.

options.text: Add `--json-schema` with a findings schema to the command, so that each run returns structured findings the `jq` step can count.
options.explanation: The schema constrains the output to a defined findings structure, so the reply is machine-parseable on every run. It adds no extra step and no waiting, which keeps the merge fast.

options.text: Send the review through the Message Batches API so that each run returns structured findings the `jq` step can count.
options.explanation: Batch results can be slow, up to 24 hours, which would block a pre-merge check. Batching is for work nothing waits on, and it does not fix the reply wrapper in the CLI.

questions.keyConcept: For machine-parseable CI output, add `--json-schema` with a findings schema rather than relying on prompt wording or cleanup.

questions.stem: Cobalt's pipeline has two jobs. Job one runs `claude -p "Implement ticket $TICKET"` and prints a session ID. Job two runs `claude -p --resume $SESSION_ID "Review the change you just made and list defects"`. Over 140 PRs the review found 2 defects, while human reviewers later found defects in 19 of the same PRs. The review must still run before each merge. Which change makes the automated review more effective?

options.text: Keep `--resume` and add the review criteria from `CLAUDE.md` and the diff to the prompt, so the reviewing session checks each changed file against them.
options.explanation: Criteria help, but the resumed session still carries the reasoning that produced the code and tends to defend it. The review remains the author checking its own work.

options.text: Run the review as a separate `claude -p` call without `--resume`, giving it the diff and the review criteria in `CLAUDE.md` and none of the author's reasoning.
options.explanation: A fresh instance has no memory of why the code was written that way, so it reads the diff critically against written criteria. It still runs before the merge, as required.

options.text: Run the review as a separate `claude -p` call without `--resume`, but pass it job one's plan and implementation notes along with the diff.
options.explanation: The call is independent, but the notes hand over the author's reasoning, which biases the reviewer toward the same assumptions. The diff and criteria alone keep the review independent.

options.text: Move the review into a nightly job that checks the day's merged changes in bulk with the Message Batches API, after the code has shipped.
options.explanation: Batch processing suits work nothing waits on, such as a weekly audit. Running after the merge means defects reach `main` first, and it does not address the review's lack of independence.

questions.keyConcept: Review with an independent Claude instance given the diff and criteria, not the author's session or its reasoning.

questions.stem: Cobalt's engineers use Claude Code locally in the monorepo. Their PCI guidance has two parts: a one-line rule, "never log a full card number", that must apply to all code, and a 25-step cardholder-data checklist needed only when someone changes `services/card-vault/`, about 3 times a month. Both sit in the root `CLAUDE.md`, adding roughly 2,500 tokens to every session. The checklist must be available to everyone on the team. How should the team split them?

options.text: Keep the one-line rule in the root `CLAUDE.md` and turn the checklist into a project skill in `.claude/skills/`, invoked whenever someone changes the vault.
options.explanation: The short rule applies to all code, so it stays always-loaded. The checklist is needed about three times a month, so an on-demand skill saves its tokens in every other session, and the project folder shares it with the team.

options.text: Keep the one-line rule in `CLAUDE.md` and turn the checklist into a personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/`, invoked when touching the vault.
options.explanation: The skill mechanism is right, but a personal skill reaches only the engineer who wrote it. The team needs the checklist when touching the vault, so it must live in the committed project folder.

options.text: Move both parts into skills so that nothing PCI-related loads until an engineer asks for it, which removes all of the 2,500 tokens.
options.explanation: The one-line rule must apply to all code, and a skill loads only when invoked. An engineer who forgets to invoke it gets no card-number rule at all, so the universal standard belongs in CLAUDE.md.

options.text: Keep both parts in `CLAUDE.md` and add a script that strips the checklist from the file unless the branch touches the vault, so other sessions stay lean.
options.explanation: Editing a committed file by script adds fragile machinery, and the file would differ between branches. A skill gives the same on-demand loading natively.

questions.keyConcept: Keep universal standards in always-loaded CLAUDE.md and move rarely needed procedures into shared project skills.

questions.stem: Developers have stopped reading Cobalt's automated PR review comments. About a third flag patterns the team's standards allow, and after each push the job posts again the comments for issues the author already fixed or dismissed. The review runs as `claude -p` with a short prompt, and the repository has no review guidance. The fix must not slow merges. Which two changes address both complaints? (Select 2.)

options.text: Ask Claude to rate each finding's confidence from 1 to 10 and post only those rated 8 or higher.
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so the threshold would drop real findings while keeping confident false ones. The problem is missing criteria, not a missing score.

options.text: Document the review criteria in `CLAUDE.md`, including which patterns the team accepts, so CI-invoked Claude Code knows what to flag.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md gives CI-invoked Claude the project's review standards. Stating which patterns are allowed removes the false positives at the source.

options.text: Run the review twice on every push and post only the findings that appear in both runs.
options.explanation: Two runs double the cost and time, and both runs still lack the criteria, so both can repeat the same false positives. Agreement between runs does not show a finding is wanted.

options.text: Include the previous review's findings in the prompt on re-runs, so Claude reports only new or still-open issues.
options.explanation: With earlier findings in the prompt, Claude can skip issues the author already fixed or dismissed. This removes the duplicate comments after each push.

options.text: Move the review to the Message Batches API so each run can examine the change at lower cost.
options.explanation: Batch results can take up to 24 hours, which would hold up a pre-merge check, and it changes nothing about what the review flags. Batching suits work that nothing is waiting on.

questions.keyConcept: Give CI-invoked Claude explicit review criteria in CLAUDE.md and prior findings on re-runs, to cut false positives and duplicates.

questions.stem: Cobalt's PCI conventions (about 80 lines) apply to `services/card-vault/`, `services/tokenizer/` and `libs/crypto/`, out of roughly 95 directories under `services/` and `libs/`. Local sessions and the CI reviewer should load them only when the work touches one of those three paths, without copies that can drift. One teammate proposes putting them in `services/CLAUDE.md`. Which approach fits the requirement?

options.text: Put the conventions in `services/CLAUDE.md`, which covers both service directories and can reference `libs/crypto/` by name.
options.explanation: A parent-directory file loads for work in all of `services/`, so about 90 unrelated directories would get the conventions. It also cannot scope `libs/crypto/` correctly. A path-scoped rule would cover all three paths exactly.

options.text: Add the conventions to the root `CLAUDE.md` under a heading for card-vault, tokenizer and crypto work, so the three areas share one file.
options.explanation: The root file loads in every session, so all engineers carry the 80 lines everywhere. A heading is only a label for Claude, not a condition on loading.

options.text: Place a copy of the conventions in a `CLAUDE.md` inside each of the three directories, keeping each in sync with the others.
options.explanation: Three copies must be kept in sync by hand, so they would drift apart. A single file with a glob list achieves the same loading with one source of truth.

options.text: Create `.claude/rules/pci.md` with frontmatter `paths: ["services/card-vault/**", "services/tokenizer/**", "libs/crypto/**"]`, so the rules load only for those paths.
options.explanation: One path-scoped rule file lists all three locations, so the conventions load only when Claude works there, in local sessions and in CI. It has no copies, so nothing can drift.

questions.keyConcept: Conventions spanning several directories belong in a path-scoped rule file, not in a parent or copied directory CLAUDE.md.

questions.stem: Cobalt's independent reviewer job runs on every PR and adds 4 minutes to checks. To speed up merges, the team moved it to run on `main` after the merge. Over the next quarter, 22 merged PRs needed follow-up fixes for defects the reviewer reported only after merge, and two of them touched card-handling services. The team still wants the 4 minutes cut, but not at the price of defects reaching `main`. What is the best approach?

options.text: Keep the reviewer running after merge, with a job that automatically reverts any merge whose review reports a defect on `main`.
options.explanation: Auto-revert cleans up after the defect has already reached `main`, and it can revert good changes on a false positive. The review's timing, not its cleanup, is what needs fixing.

options.text: Restore the reviewer as a blocking pre-merge check on every PR, an independent `claude -p` run on the PR diff with criteria in `CLAUDE.md`.
options.explanation: A blocking pre-merge review stops defects before they reach `main`. Limiting it to the diff with written criteria keeps the run short, and an independent instance keeps it unbiased.

options.text: Run the reviewer nightly across the day's merges with the Message Batches API instead of a blocking pre-merge check, which costs less than a synchronous run.
options.explanation: Batch fits work nothing waits on, such as a nightly audit. A nightly run finds defects a day after merge, so the 22 follow-up fixes would continue.

options.text: Let the author's own session review its change as a pre-merge step before opening the PR, since its context is already loaded and no new job is needed.
options.explanation: The author's session is less effective at spotting its own mistakes because it carries the reasoning behind them. Removing the independent job saves the 4 minutes but loses the reviewer's value.

questions.keyConcept: Review that must gate a merge runs synchronously and independently before the merge; batch review suits only work nothing waits on.

questions.stem: A Cobalt engineer asked Claude for `round_fee()`, which rounds card processing fees. His prose spec says "round to the nearest cent, rounding halves the way our ledger does". The results vary between runs: the decimal `0.125` sometimes becomes `0.12` and sometimes `0.13`, while the ledger expects `0.12` for `0.125` and `0.14` for `0.135`. He needs it merged before month-end close, but the results must be consistent. Which change gives consistent results?

options.text: Add a paragraph to the spec that explains how the ledger rounds halves, with the theory behind it, and ask Claude to follow it exactly.
options.explanation: More prose is the same kind of input that was already interpreted two ways. Concrete examples show the tie-breaking rule directly and leave much less room for reading it differently.

options.text: Give Claude two or three input and output examples, such as `0.125 -> 0.12` and `0.135 -> 0.14`, and ask it to match every one.
options.explanation: Examples that include several halves show the exact tie-breaking rule, so Claude can infer it instead of guessing. Two or three varied cases are enough, and they can double as tests.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature for the session so that repeated runs of the same prompt produce the same code on each run.
options.explanation: A lower temperature may make runs more alike, but it would lock in whichever interpretation of "the way our ledger does" Claude chose first, which may be the wrong one.

options.text: Give Claude one example, `0.125 -> 0.12`, as a reference for the ledger's rule and ask it to match that example.
options.explanation: A single example fits several rules, such as always rounding halves down, and it says nothing about `0.135`. Varied examples that include a half going up pin the rule down.

questions.keyConcept: When prose is interpreted inconsistently, give two or three concrete input and output examples that pin down the rule.
